summary:
MARSWALK is a console application for offline EVA planning of Gale Crater and the lower slopes of Mount Sharp, where NASA’s Curiosity rover operated since 2012. It solves an important problem for the astronaut: Can I walk to this rock and come back safely?

The algorithm estimates the walk-back time to the nearest safe haven from each terrain grid cell using real HiRISE stereo topography. The algorithm utilizes Tobler’s hiking function with different costs for uphill and downhill traversing. Any traversing plan that exceeds consumables is automatically rejected, providing the constraint violated and corresponding time difference.

The system includes NASA datasets: 1 m/pixel HiRISE stereo DTM from PDS, 18 m/pixel CRISM MTRDR parameters, 1,039 Curiosity waypoints (Sols 1167-5073), and RAD surface radiation measurements. Each dataset is labeled either “Real, Derived or Modeled” and their limitations are discussed. In addition, derived geochemical units are validated according to NASA stratigraphy.

Only 8.2 MB of data is used, which allows operating the whole console without internet connection, just like on planet Mars.
details:
What it does

MARSWALK transforms NASA’s orbital and rover data to develop an extravehicular activity (EVA) planning tool for the 6.77 by 14.62 km stretch of Gale Crater terrain that spans Curiosity’s journey from the Glen Torridon clay formation to Gediz Vallis and the 2025 boxwork expedition.

The user specifies the science targets, a space suit model, the hour of departure and a dust condition. MARSWALK provides a GO or NO-GO decision along with the mathematics of the calculation: the distance traveled, time taken, resources left, total dose equivalent and number of minutes of margin sacrificed to the cold.

How it works

The core is a walk-back field. A single multi-source Dijkstra search starts from every safe haven at once and relaxes outward across the grid until each cell knows its cheapest way back. Travel time is calculated from the Tobler’s hiking function on terrain gradients obtained by the Horn 3×3 operator, and is directional – walking upwards along a slope is different from walking downwards along it. A route is GO if the sum of its return time, task duration, and thermal penalty is less than the reserve of consumables.

Temperature is a variable that drives the result, not a number shown on a panel. It is modelled from published REMS values for Gale Crater, and labelled MODELED in the interface. The suit heating system consumes more power in cold air temperatures, increasing consumables burn rate, and adds a cold-soak penalty at egress. Egressing at dusk is a costly decision compared to midday.

Geochemistry drives the science, not the terrain cost. There are nine thresholded CRISM summary parameters defining five geochemical units, with thresholds computed per scene, and specific investigations and associated durations for each unit. Drilling is not sampling, which in turn is not imaging. We purposely refrain from calculating walking cost through geochemistry; clay index describes a certain spectral shape, but not the bearing strength of the ground.

The problem we solve

A map tells you where you are. It does not tell you what you can still do. On a Mars surface EVA there is no rescue, no second vehicle, and no margin for a bad estimate, so the question that decides every traverse is not “how far is that outcrop?” but “if I walk to it and something fails, can I still get back before my consumables run out?”

That question is harder than it looks, for three reasons. The return is not symmetric with the outbound: an easy downhill walk out becomes an uphill climb back, at a different speed and a different burn rate. The answer changes with what the crew intends to do when they arrive, because a drilling campaign and an imaging pass consume very different amounts of the same clock. And it changes with the hour of the day, because suit heating power scales with ambient temperature, in our default plan, the cold alone costs 20 minutes of margin.

In practice these live in separate places: topography in one map viewer, mineralogy in another, consumables and timeline in a spreadsheet, and the walk-back calculation in somebody’s head. MARSWALK was built because the number that actually governs crew safety, the return time from the furthest point of the plan, is the one number none of those tools computes.

What MARSWALK provides

The walk-back field. Rather than evaluating one route at a time, the planner solves the return for the entire area at once: a multi-source Dijkstra search starts from every safe haven simultaneously and relaxes outward across the terrain grid, using Tobler’s hiking function over slopes derived with a Horn 3×3 operator, with uphill and downhill costed differently. When it settles, every cell on the map carries the cost of its own cheapest way home. GO/NO-GO therefore becomes a property of the ground, not of a route someone already drew, and the whole plan re-solves the instant anything changes.

That turns planning into something a crew can argue with. Our default traverse is GO at 7.92 km, 4:51, with 26% of consumables left. Add one station at Gediz Vallis Ridge and it becomes NO-GO, not with a red light, but with the rule and the arithmetic: 71 minutes short of the reserve on an abort from that station, and 22 minutes of consumables remaining against a 96-minute reserve requirement. Select clay mineralogy as the investigation instead, and the same route fails for a different reason: 95 minutes of drilling per station pushes 4:51 to 5:56 and 26% to 13%. The science objective, the terrain and the clock are solved together because on a real EVA they are not separable.

Trust you can audit. An EVA tool that hides its uncertainty is more dangerous than no tool, because a crew would act on it. Every layer is labelled REAL (downloaded from a NASA archive), DERIVED (computed by us) or MODELED (built from published measurements), and the app states what each source cannot tell you. Where the HiRISE stereo pair has no coverage, 25.2% of the area, those cells are barred from routing rather than interpolated; the planner refuses to walk over ground it cannot see. We also publish our own failures: our derived geochemical units do not reproduce the published clay-below-sulfate ordering on Mount Sharp, our detections are 1.46× more vertically structured than the control (residual instrument striping, not mineralogy), and a pooled-threshold bug we found and fixed had made the unit map a picture of which observation covered what. All of it is measured, written into the shipped data, and shown on screen.

Finally, the whole pipeline resolves offline into 8.2 MB of static data. Nothing is fetched at run time, which is both why the demo cannot fail on a conference network, and the condition a crew on the surface would actually be working under.

What we were careful about

Of the area that does have stereo coverage, 58.4% is walkable. As noted above, our derived units do not reproduce the published stratigraphy of Mount Sharp — and that is not left as a remark. Three validation tests are performed during each build: cross-scene consistency, stratigraphic order and slope dependence, and their results, including any failures, are provided in the shipped data and the user interface. The build stops if there is a difference of 10× or greater between the rate of classification in two different scenes, as this very mistake caused us to produce a map of observed scenes rather than geological features.

The sources that were not used are listed along with the reasons, in scripts/sources.json. The CRISM global mosaic (180 m/px) and the USGS global geologic map (1:20,000,000) are both real datasets, and both are too coarse for this question: a single pixel of the mosaic spans several science stations, and the entire 6.77 × 14.62 km area is smaller than one unit of the geologic map. We could have easily used the ready-to-go browse rasters of CRISM, but they are 8-bit renderings, and the contrast for each scene is adjusted separately, therefore the scenes are not comparable.

Tools

Frontend: TypeScript (strict mode), React 19, Vite 7, Tailwind CSS v4, Leaflet 1.9 for the 2D map, three.js through react-three-fiber for the 3D terrain, Zustand for state management.

Data pipeline: Python 3.11 with numpy, pillow and requests but no GDAL. Products from the PDS archives are accessed directly using HTTP range requests, allowing us to download a 540 MB digital terrain model and 139 MB spectral cube as just a few megabytes of the actual row and band slices that we care about. The PDS3 labels and ENVI headers are manually parsed; band order is extracted dynamically from the header rather than hard-coded, while the georeference is verified independently through two separate channels (detached PDS label and ENVI map info).

Impact

There is no rescue for a surface EVA on Mars; the critical factor is not distance but the trip back. The cost of going back is not symmetrical with the cost of the trip out. It is the difference between a plan that treats the return as the governing constraint — and knows which of its numbers are measured and which are inferred — and a plan that merely looks confident. We built the first kind on purpose: everywhere the app shows an inference, it says so.
